Solution of the Mumford–Shah conjecture

Francesco Deangelis Address: Applied Mathematics Münster, University of Münster, Einsteinstrasse 62, 48149 Münster, Germany Email address: francesco.deangelis@uni-muenster.de
Abstract.

We prove the Mumford–Shah conjecture, formulated in 1989, by completing the classification of blow-up limits of minimizers in the plane. The remaining case concerns limits whose discontinuity set is noncompact and has connected complement. In this setting, we rule out bounded connected components using second-variation inequalities obtained from combined inner and outer variations associated with two perpendicular translations of a compact subset separated from the rest of the discontinuity set. Established results then imply that the discontinuity set is connected, and the known classification for connected discontinuity sets completes the proof.

1. Introduction and main result

The Mumford–Shah functional was introduced as a variational model for image segmentation [MS89]. Its unknowns are a function uu, representing a piecewise smooth approximation of a given image gg, and a set KK, representing its edges. The model balances the Dirichlet energy of uu away from KK, the length of KK, and the discrepancy between uu and the image. This competition leads to a free discontinuity problem: both the function and the set across which it may jump are determined by minimization.

Let Ω⊂ℝ2\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be open, let g∈L∞​(Ω,ℝ)g\in L^{\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb{R}), and let λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. For a relatively closed, countably ℋ1\mathcal{H}^{1}-rectifiable set K⊂ΩK\subset\Omega and a function u∈Wloc1,2​(Ω∖K,ℝ)u\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega\setminus K;\mathbb{R}), we consider

ℰλ​(u,K,U)=∫U∖K(|∇u|2+λ​|u−g|2)​⁡𝑑x+ℋ1​(K∩U)\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}(u,K;U)=\int_{U\setminus K}\bigl(|\nabla u|^{2}+\lambda|u-g|^{2}\bigr)\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x+\mathcal{H}^{1}(K\cap U) (1.1)

for bounded open sets U⊂ΩU\subset\Omega. The term λ​∫U∖K|u−g|2​⁡𝑑x\lambda\int_{U\setminus K}|u-g|^{2}\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x is called the fidelity term: it penalizes the discrepancy between uu and the prescribed datum gg, with weight λ\lambda. The Dirichlet term penalizes large spatial gradients, whereas the length term makes discontinuities costly; allowing jumps can, however, reduce the cost of approximating sharp transitions in gg.

The central regularity question concerns the geometry of the minimizing set KK. The conjecture of Mumford and Shah predicts that, in the interior of the domain, KK is a locally finite union of C1C^{1} arcs, which may have free endpoints and may meet only in triple junctions with angles of 120∘120^{\circ}. Thus a point of KK should have precisely one of three local configurations: a regular arc, a loose end, or a triple junction. The difficulty is to derive this description from minimality without assuming in advance that KK is connected, has finitely many components, or already consists of curves. In this paper we prove the planar interior conjecture by completing the classification of generalized global minimizers.

Background and earlier results

The existence theory rests on formulations that allow discontinuity sets with no prescribed smoothness. De Giorgi and Ambrosio [DGA88] introduced the space of special functions of bounded variation, and Ambrosio [Amb90] developed an existence theory for free discontinuity energies in this setting. The density estimates and essential closedness theorem of De Giorgi, Carriero and Leaci [DGCL89] link the weak formulation to minimization over pairs (u,K)(u,K) with KK closed. Dal Maso, Morel and Solimini [DMMS92] developed a complementary geometric approach to existence and approximation. These results provide a framework in which the regularity conjecture can be studied without building its conclusion into the admissible class; see also [AFP].

A major part of the subsequent theory consists of ε\varepsilon-regularity results: sufficiently good approximation by an expected model at one scale implies regularity at smaller scales. David [Dav96] established such results near straight lines and triple junctions. The work of Ambrosio–Pallara [AP97] and Ambrosio–Fusco–Pallara [AFP97] developed partial regularity in arbitrary dimension. In particular, the discontinuity set of a planar minimizer is locally a regular arc at ℋ1\mathcal{H}^{1}-almost every point. This almost-everywhere description does not by itself control the exceptional points or exclude the accumulation of small connected components.

The loose-end case required a further development. Even when the set was known to consist of a single arc ending at an interior point, the existence of a tangent at that endpoint was a separate issue. De Lellis, Focardi and Ghinassi [DLFG21] proved an ε\varepsilon-regularity theorem near the crack-tip model, establishing regularity up to the loose end and vanishing curvature there; see also the earlier work of Andersson and Mikayelyan [AM19]. The treatment of the fidelity term, together with a unified account of the planar theory, is given in the monograph of De Lellis and Focardi [DLF]. Earlier systematic accounts include [Dav05]. Another line of progress concerns higher integrability: De Lellis and Focardi [DLF13] proved that ∇u\nabla u belongs locally to LpL^{p} for some p>2p>2 in the plane, and De Philippis and Figalli [DPF14] established the corresponding result in arbitrary dimension.

Further contributions to the regularity theory include higher regularity of the regular part of the discontinuity set [AFP99], flatness and finiteness results [Leg99], quantitative density lower bounds [LF13], and monotonicity formulae for more general free discontinuity problems [BL14]. For planar minimizers of the fidelity-free functional, Fischer [Fis22] obtained a monotonicity formula for the David–Léger entropy truncated at the sharp level 3/23/2, without a connectedness assumption on the discontinuity set, and derived an optimal lower bound on the energy density at points where uu is not smooth. In dimension three, regularity near minimal cones [Lem11], rigidity of global minimizers [Lem15], and stationarity of crack-front configurations [LM18] have also been investigated. More recently, Zhang [Zha25] gave an alternative proof of a local square-root growth estimate at tip points, extending an estimate of David and Léger. Labourie and Lemenant [LL26] proved that a planar minimizer uu has at most three distinct limit values at each point of KK, when approached from Ω∖K\Omega\setminus K, answering a question of De Giorgi.

The connection between local regularity and global geometry comes from blow-up analysis. The rescaling

Kx,r=K−xr,ux,r(y)=r−1/2u(x+ry)K_{x,r}=\frac{K-x}{r},\qquad u_{x,r}(y)=r^{-1/2}u(x+ry)

puts the Dirichlet energy and the length on the same scale:

ℰ0​(ux,r,Kx,r,BR)=r−1​ℰ0​(u,K,Br​R​(x)).\mathcal{E}_{0}(u_{x,r},K_{x,r};B_{R})=r^{-1}\mathcal{E}_{0}(u,K;B_{rR}(x)).

The fidelity term disappears in the limit as r↓0r\downarrow 0. Compactness, with suitable normalizations of the additive constants on different complementary components, leads to generalized global minimizers of the fidelity-free energy. The expected models are the constant configuration, the pure jump across a straight line, the triple junction, and the crack tip. The latter consists of a half-line and a function with square-root growth; its precise normalization is recalled in (2.2). The compactness and ε\varepsilon-regularity theory makes the interior conjecture equivalent to the assertion that these models exhaust the generalized global minimizers [DLF, Theorem 1.4.5].

Several fundamental classification results establish this assertion under additional geometric hypotheses. Bonnet [Bon96] introduced a monotonicity argument and classified global minimizers whose discontinuity set is connected. Bonnet and David [BD01] proved that the crack tip is globally minimizing and obtained a stronger rigidity theorem, which applies when all but at most one connected component of KK are contained in a common compact set. David and Léger [DL02] classified the case in which KK disconnects the plane, leaving only the straight line and the triple junction, and showed that KK has at most one unbounded connected component. The forms of these results used below are recalled in Section 2. Together they isolate the remaining difficulty in configurations with disconnected KK and connected complement, for which bounded components cannot all be confined to one compact set.

There is also a related regularity problem at the boundary of the ambient domain. For prescribed Dirichlet data, the author [Dea24] studied boundary blow-ups and proved an ε\varepsilon-regularity theorem near the tangent line to the boundary. The result proved here concerns interior points; the boundary problem involves a different class of limiting minimizers.

Main result

We now specify the local minimality convention in the statement. We call (u,K)(u,K) admissible if its energy is locally finite, that is, ℰλ​(u,K,U)<∞\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}(u,K;U)<\infty for every open U⋐ΩU\Subset\Omega. We call an admissible pair (u,K)(u,K) an absolute minimizer if, for every bounded open U⊂ΩU\subset\Omega,

ℰλ​(u,K,U)≤ℰλ​(v,L,U)\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}(u,K;U)\leq\mathcal{E}_{\lambda}(v,L;U)

for every admissible (v,L)(v,L) for which some compact C⊂UC\subset U satisfies

L∖C=K∖C,v=ua.e. on Ω∖(C∪K∪L).L\setminus C=K\setminus C,\qquad v=u\quad\text{a.e. on }\Omega\setminus(C\cup K\cup L). (1.2)

This is absolute minimality in [DLF, Section 1.1 and Definition 1.2.1]; competitor sets LL are rectifiable, but there is no restriction on their topology. We call KK reduced if

ℋ1​(K∩Br​(x))>0whenever ​x∈K​ and ​Br​(x)¯⊂Ω.\mathcal{H}^{1}(K\cap B_{r}(x))>0\quad\text{whenever }x\in K\text{ and }\overline{B_{r}(x)}\subset\Omega. (1.3)

When Ω=ℝ2\Omega=\mathbb{R}^{2}, the same definition is used in every ball. This condition requires KK to coincide locally with the support of its length measure, excluding extraneous points that would obscure a geometric statement.

Theorem 1.1 (Planar interior regularity).

Let (u,K)(u,K) be an absolute minimizer of (1.1), and suppose that KK is reduced. For every x∈Kx\in K there are r>0r>0 with Br​(x)¯⊂Ω\overline{B_{r}(x)}\subset\Omega, an integer m∈{1,2,3}m\in\{1,2,3\}, positive numbers ℓ1,…,ℓm\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{m}, and injective maps

γi∈C1([0,ℓi];ℝ2),i=1,…,m,\gamma_{i}\in C^{1}([0,\ell_{i}];\mathbb{R}^{2}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,

with

|γi′​(s)|=1(0≤s≤ℓi),γi​(0)=x,\displaystyle|\gamma_{i}^{\prime}(s)|=1\quad(0\leq s\leq\ell_{i}),\qquad\gamma_{i}(0)=x, (1.4)
γi​(ℓi)∈∂Br​(x),γi​([0,ℓi))⊂Br​(x),\displaystyle\gamma_{i}(\ell_{i})\in\partial B_{r}(x),\qquad\gamma_{i}([0,\ell_{i}))\subset B_{r}(x),
K∩Br​(x)¯=⋃i=1mγi​([0,ℓi]),\displaystyle K\cap\overline{B_{r}(x)}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\gamma_{i}([0,\ell_{i}]), (1.5)
γi​([0,ℓi])∩γj​([0,ℓj])={x}(i≠j).\displaystyle\gamma_{i}([0,\ell_{i}])\cap\gamma_{j}([0,\ell_{j}])=\{x\}\qquad(i\neq j).

Endpoint derivatives are one-sided. The outward unit tangents τi=γi′​(0)\tau_{i}=\gamma_{i}^{\prime}(0) satisfy

τ1+τ2=0(m=2),τi⋅τj=−12(i≠j,m=3).\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}=0\quad(m=2),\qquad\tau_{i}\cdot\tau_{j}=-\frac{1}{2}\quad(i\neq j,\ m=3). (1.6)

Outline of the proof

The proof reduces to the classification of reduced generalized global minimizers. By the established results recalled above, it remains to consider noncompact KK with connected complement ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K. Our strategy is to use second variations to exclude bounded connected components of KK. Indeed, the David–Léger theorem gives at most one unbounded component; once every component is unbounded, KK is connected and the known classification applies.

A bounded connected component need not be isolated from the other components, so it cannot necessarily be translated independently. However, Lemma 3.3 shows that it is contained in a nonempty compact subset S⊂KS\subset K which is both open and closed relative to KK. Since KK is noncompact, SS is a proper subset of KK. Moreover, compactness of SS and closedness of K∖SK\setminus S imply that the two sets have positive distance. We can therefore translate SS while keeping the rest of KK fixed, preserving its length. Proposition 3.1 rules out such a set by combining the second-variation inequalities for two perpendicular translations, while allowing uu to adjust to each deformation.

Our starting point, Lemma 3.2, is a second-variation estimate for a generalized global minimizer with connected complement D=ℝ2∖KD=\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K, valid for every deformation field X∈Cc∞​(ℝ2,ℝ2)X\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}). No smoothness of KK in the region affected by the deformation is required. We consider the combined inner and outer variations

Φt=Id+t​X,Kt=Φt​(K),ut∘Φt=u+t​φ,\Phi_{t}=\operatorname{Id}+tX,\qquad K_{t}=\Phi_{t}(K),\qquad u_{t}\circ\Phi_{t}=u+t\varphi,

where φ∈𝒯K\varphi\in\mathscr{T}_{K} and

𝒯K={φ∈W1,2​(D):φ=0​ a.e. outside some compact subset of ​ℝ2}.\mathscr{T}_{K}=\{\varphi\in W^{1,2}(D):\varphi=0\text{ a.e. outside some compact subset of }\mathbb{R}^{2}\}.

The coefficient of t2t^{2} in the energy expansion is

QX+‖∇φ‖22+2​⟨mX,∇φ⟩.Q_{X}+\|\nabla\varphi\|_{2}^{2}+2\langle m_{X},\nabla\varphi\rangle.

Here QXQ_{X} is the coefficient for the pure inner variation, obtained by setting φ=0\varphi=0, while mXm_{X} couples the deformation to the correction of uu through the inner product ⟨mX,∇φ⟩\langle m_{X},\nabla\varphi\rangle above. Explicitly,

mX\displaystyle m_{X} =((divX)I−DX−(DX)T)∇u,\displaystyle=\bigl((\operatorname{div}X)I-DX-(DX)^{T}\bigr)\nabla u,
QX\displaystyle Q_{X} =∫D(|(DX)T∇u|2−det(DX)|∇u|2)dx\displaystyle=\int_{D}\bigl(|(DX)^{T}\nabla u|^{2}-\det(DX)|\nabla u|^{2}\bigr)\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}x
+12∫K(|DXτ|2−(τ⋅DXτ)2)dℋ1,\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{K}\bigl(|DX\,\tau|^{2}-(\tau\cdot DX\,\tau)^{2}\bigr)\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{1},

where τ\tau is a unit approximate tangent to KK. Norms and inner products are taken in L2​(ℝ2,ℝ2)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}).

For each fixed XX, inner variations alone give QX≥0Q_{X}\geq 0. The freedom to choose φ\varphi gives a stronger condition: completing the square and taking the infimum over φ∈𝒯K\varphi\in\mathscr{T}_{K} yields

QX≥‖ΠK​mX‖22,Q_{X}\geq\|\Pi_{K}m_{X}\|_{2}^{2},

where ΠK\Pi_{K} is the orthogonal projection onto the L2L^{2} closure of the gradients of functions in 𝒯K\mathscr{T}_{K}. Thus the optimization quantifies how much the quadratic cost of a prescribed deformation can be reduced by adjusting uu.

Second variations of the Mumford–Shah functional were also studied by Cagnetti, Mora and Morini [CMM08]. Their analysis concerns deformations supported in the regular part of the discontinuity set, with the function chosen to minimize the Dirichlet energy on the deformed domain with fixed boundary values.

We then apply this general estimate to X1=χ​e1X_{1}=\chi e_{1} and X2=χ​e2X_{2}=\chi e_{2}, where χ\chi is a smooth compactly supported cutoff equal to one near SS and zero near K∖SK\setminus S. These fields generate the two perpendicular translations of SS. Their pure inner quadratic costs QX1Q_{X_{1}} and QX2Q_{X_{2}} are already nonnegative, so the essential information comes from the projection term obtained by optimizing over φ\varphi. The associated fields mX1m_{X_{1}} and mX2m_{X_{2}} are related by a 90∘90^{\circ} rotation and satisfy

QX1+QX2=‖mX1‖22=‖mX2‖22.Q_{X_{1}}+Q_{X_{2}}=\|m_{X_{1}}\|_{2}^{2}=\|m_{X_{2}}\|_{2}^{2}.

Let Π\Pi denote the orthogonal projection onto the L2L^{2} closure of the gradients of functions in Cc∞​(ℝ2)C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}). The Hodge decomposition on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} gives

‖Π​mX1‖22+‖Π​mX2‖22=QX1+QX2.\|\Pi m_{X_{1}}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\Pi m_{X_{2}}\|_{2}^{2}=Q_{X_{1}}+Q_{X_{2}}.

Since the restrictions to DD of functions in Cc∞​(ℝ2)C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) belong to 𝒯K\mathscr{T}_{K}, the space defining Π\Pi is contained in the space defining ΠK\Pi_{K}. Thus replacing Π\Pi by ΠK\Pi_{K} can only increase each squared norm. On the other hand, the second-variation inequalities bound ‖ΠK​mXi‖22\|\Pi_{K}m_{X_{i}}\|_{2}^{2} by QXiQ_{X_{i}} for i=1,2i=1,2. Summing these inequalities forces equality throughout. Let vv be a real scalar potential such that

∇v=Π​mX1.\nabla v=\Pi m_{X_{1}}.

It satisfies Δ​v=div⁡mX1\Delta v=\operatorname{div}m_{X_{1}}, so it is harmonic near KK, where mX1=0m_{X_{1}}=0. The equality conditions imply that both the normal and tangential derivatives of vv vanish along every regular arc of KK. Thus ∇v=0\nabla v=0 on these arcs.

To connect this information back to uu, we use the equation for the potential to split one derivative of uu into two harmonic functions. One extends through SS and the other through K∖SK\setminus S. The vanishing conditions and unique continuation make both functions constant. It follows that ∇u\nabla u is constant, and the linear energy-growth bound forces it to vanish. The classification of minimizers with vanishing Dirichlet energy then contradicts the presence of SS.

This excludes bounded connected components in the remaining case and completes the classification in Theorem 3.4. The planar regularity statement, Theorem 1.1, then follows by the existing compactness and regularity theory, including regularity at loose ends.

Section 2 records the precise results from that theory needed for this implication. Section 3 proves compact translation rigidity and its topological consequence, and completes the global classification.

2. Reduction to a global classification

All references to the established theory below use the published monograph [DLF].

We use generalized global minimizer exactly as in [DLF, Definition 2.2.4]: it is a triple (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}) arising from rescaled absolute minimizers. The extended-real parameters pk​lp_{kl} record relative additive constants on the connected components of ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K. They are part of the definition; when ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K is connected, the only parameter is p11=0p_{11}=0.

The compactness theorem below requires a uniform L∞L^{\infty} bound on the minimizers before rescaling [DLF, Assumption 2.2.1(iv)]. For blow-ups of a fixed absolute minimizer (u,K)(u,K) at an interior point, we obtain this bound by working on a sufficiently small ball. The maximum principle [DLF, Lemma 2.1.1] gives local boundedness of uu when λ>0\lambda>0. When λ=0\lambda=0, a local truncation gives a bounded function u~\widetilde{u} such that (u~,K)(\widetilde{u},K) is still an absolute minimizer and ∇u~=∇u\nabla\widetilde{u}=\nabla u. We apply the compactness theorem to this bounded minimizer.

The compactness theorem [DLF, Theorem 2.2.3] supplies a generalized global limit (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}) along a subsequence of every sequence of interior rescalings. It gives local Hausdorff convergence to KK and separate convergence of Dirichlet energies and length measures. The limiting set KK is reduced, countably ℋ1\mathcal{H}^{1}-rectifiable, and locally of finite length, while u∈W1,2​(BR∖K)u\in W^{1,2}(B_{R}\setminus K) for every R>0R>0. For every generalized global minimizer (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}), the upper density bound [DLF, Lemma 2.1.2] gives

∫BR​(z)∖K|∇u|2+ℋ1​(K∩BR​(z))≤2​π​R(z∈ℝ2,R>0).\int_{B_{R}(z)\setminus K}|\nabla u|^{2}+\mathcal{H}^{1}(K\cap B_{R}(z))\leq 2\pi R\qquad(z\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\ R>0). (2.1)

Moreover, [DLF, Corollary 3.1.5] gives a relatively open subset of regular points of KK of full ℋ1\mathcal{H}^{1} measure. At each such point xx, there is r>0r>0 such that K∩Br​(x)K\cap B_{r}(x) is a single embedded C1C^{1} arc.

If D=ℝ2∖KD=\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K is connected, the exterior separation condition on competitors in [DLF, Definition 2.2.2] is vacuous. Consequently [DLF, Theorem 2.2.3(ii)] makes (u,K)(u,K) an ordinary absolute minimizer of the fidelity-free energy on the plane. In particular, the compactly supported combined inner and outer variations used in Section 3 are admissible.

A generalized global minimizer (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}) is called elementary if ∇u=0\nabla u=0 almost everywhere on ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K. By [DLF, Theorem 2.4.1], in this case KK is either empty, a straight line (the pure-jump model), or the union of three half-lines with a common endpoint and pairwise angles of 120∘120^{\circ} (the triple-junction model). In each case, uu is constant on every connected component of ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K. The other canonical model is the crack tip. Up to translation, rotation, sign, and an additive constant, its set KK and function uu are given by

K={(r,0):r≥0},u(r,θ)=2πrcosθ2,r>0,0<θ<2π.\begin{gathered}K=\{(r,0):r\geq 0\},\\ u(r,\theta)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\sqrt{r}\cos\frac{\theta}{2},\quad r>0,\quad 0<\theta<2\pi.\end{gathered} (2.2)

The parameters pk​lp_{kl} in the two disconnected models are interpreted as in [DLF, Section 2.4]. For a generalized global minimizer (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}), we shall use the following classification results:

  1. (i)

    If ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K is disconnected, then ∇u=0\nabla u=0 almost everywhere on ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K, and KK is either a straight line or the triple-junction configuration described above [DLF, Theorem 4.4.1].

  2. (ii)

    KK has at most one unbounded connected component [DLF, Corollary 4.4.3].

  3. (iii)

    If all but at most one connected component of KK lie in one common compact set, then the minimizer is elementary or (u,K)(u,K) is the canonical crack tip (2.2), up to the transformations specified above [DLF, Theorem 1.4.6, first paragraph].

These are the established David–Léger and Bonnet–David classification results, in the form needed for generalized limits.

By [DLF, Theorem 1.4.5], it suffices to prove the classification stated in Theorem 3.4. After the usual local normalization and rescaling, the regularity theorem [DLF, Theorem 1.3.3] gives Theorem 1.1. Along each sufficiently short C1C^{1} branch issuing from xx, the distance from xx increases strictly. We may therefore choose a smaller ball whose boundary meets each branch exactly once. Parametrizing the resulting closed arcs by arclength gives (1.4)–(1.5). The local description at every point of KK also gives a neighborhood containing no endpoints or triple junctions other than, possibly, that point itself. Since KK is relatively closed in Ω\Omega, such points cannot accumulate in Ω\Omega and are therefore locally finite.

3. Compact translations and global classification

We first prove the compact translation rigidity result and then use it to complete the classification of generalized global minimizers.

3.1. Admissible variations and optimization over corrections

For a closed set K⊂ℝ2K\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} of zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure, put D=ℝ2∖KD=\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K and define the real test space

𝒯K={φ∈W1,2​(D):φ=0​ a.e. outside some compact subset of ​ℝ2}.\mathscr{T}_{K}=\{\varphi\in W^{1,2}(D):\varphi=0\text{ a.e. outside some compact subset of }\mathbb{R}^{2}\}.

We shall use the closed subspace

𝒱K={∇φ:φ∈𝒯K}¯L2​(ℝ2,ℝ2)\mathcal{V}_{K}=\overline{\{\nabla\varphi:\varphi\in\mathscr{T}_{K}\}}^{\,L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2})}

and its orthogonal projection ΠK\Pi_{K}. Sets of zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure are ignored when identifying vector fields on DD with vector fields on the plane.

Let (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}) be a generalized global minimizer with ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K connected. Absolute minimality gives the weak equation

∫D∇u⋅∇φ=0(φ∈𝒯K)\int_{D}\nabla u\cdot\nabla\varphi=0\qquad(\varphi\in\mathscr{T}_{K}) (3.1)

and the inner variation identity

∫D(|∇u|2divX−2∇u⋅DX∇u)+∫Kτ⋅DXτdℋ1=0.\int_{D}\bigl(|\nabla u|^{2}\operatorname{div}X-2\nabla u\cdot DX\nabla u\bigr)+\int_{K}\tau\cdot DX\tau\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathcal{H}^{1}=0. (3.2)

Here X∈Cc∞​(ℝ2,ℝ2)X\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}) and τ\tau is a unit approximate tangent to KK. These are the usual variational identities; see [DLF, Section 2.5]. Minimality also gives second-order stability under the combined inner and outer variations

Φt=Id+t​X,Kt=Φt​(K),ut∘Φt=u+t​φ.\Phi_{t}=\operatorname{Id}+tX,\qquad K_{t}=\Phi_{t}(K),\qquad u_{t}\circ\Phi_{t}=u+t\varphi. (3.3)

These reduce to inner variations when φ=0\varphi=0 and to outer variations when X=0X=0. Differences of the infinite global energies are evaluated on a bounded region containing the support of the variation.

Proposition 3.1 (Compact translation rigidity).

Let (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}) be a reduced generalized global minimizer with ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K connected. There is no nonempty compact proper subset of KK which is both open and closed relative to KK.

Lemma 3.2 (Second variation optimized over corrections to uu).

Let (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}) be a generalized global minimizer with ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K connected. For X∈Cc∞​(ℝ2,ℝ2)X\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2};\mathbb{R}^{2}), define

3.2. Two translations and the Hodge decomposition

Harmonic separation of the compact piece

We use the following standard harmonic uniqueness fact: if ww is harmonic on a connected open set U⊂ℝ2U\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} and ∇w=0\nabla w=0 along a nontrivial embedded C1C^{1} arc contained in UU, then ww is constant. Indeed, w=cw=c and ∂νw=0\partial_{\nu}w=0 on a connected subarc. Extending w−cw-c from one side by zero to the other gives a weakly harmonic function in a small neighborhood, by integration by parts. Interior elliptic regularity and the identity principle imply that this extension vanishes. Thus w=cw=c on an open subset of UU, and hence throughout UU.

Using uy​y=−ux​xu_{yy}=-u_{xx} and ux​y=uy​xu_{xy}=u_{yx} in (3.8), we compute on DD

divm=−(Δχ)ux−2∇χ⋅∇ux=−Δ(χux).\operatorname{div}m=-(\Delta\chi)u_{x}-2\nabla\chi\cdot\nabla u_{x}=-\Delta(\chi u_{x}). (3.15)

are harmonic on DD and satisfy f0+f1=uxf_{0}+f_{1}=u_{x}. Near SS, the first equals −v-v, so it extends harmonically through SS. Near K∖SK\setminus S, the second equals vv, so it extends harmonically through K∖SK\setminus S. Their respective domains of extension are

U0=ℝ2∖(K∖S),U1=ℝ2∖S.U_{0}=\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus(K\setminus S),\qquad U_{1}=\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus S.

Both domains are connected: each contains connected DD, and every open component meets DD because KK has zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

By (3.7) and full-measure regularity, SS contains a regular subarc. Near that subarc f0=−vf_{0}=-v, and (3.14) gives ∇f0=0\nabla f_{0}=0 there. The harmonic uniqueness fact therefore makes f0f_{0} constant throughout U0U_{0}. The nonempty relatively open set K∖SK\setminus S also contains a positive-length regular subarc, by reducedness and full-measure regularity. Near it f1=vf_{1}=v, so the same argument makes f1f_{1} constant throughout U1U_{1}.

It follows that ux=f0+f1u_{x}=f_{0}+f_{1} is constant on DD. Harmonicity gives

∇uy=(ux​y,uy​y)=(0,−ux​x)=0.\nabla u_{y}=(u_{xy},u_{yy})=(0,-u_{xx})=0.

Connectedness of DD then makes uyu_{y} constant as well. Thus ∇u\nabla u is a constant vector on DD. Since KK has zero two-dimensional Lebesgue measure, a nonzero constant gradient would give quadratic bulk-energy growth, contrary to (2.1). Consequently ∇u=0\nabla u=0 on DD. By the classification of elementary generalized global minimizers [DLF, Theorem 2.4.1], connectedness of DD implies K=∅K=\varnothing, contradicting ∅≠S⊂K\varnothing\neq S\subset K. This proves the proposition. ∎

3.3. Topological consequence and classification

Lemma 3.3.

Let K⊂ℝ2K\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be closed. If KK has no nonempty compact subset that is both relatively open and relatively closed in KK, then every connected component of KK is unbounded.

Proof.

Suppose that CC is a bounded connected component of KK. Since CC is closed in KK and KK is closed in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, the set CC is closed and bounded in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, hence compact. Choose RR with C⊂BRC\subset B_{R} and set

X:=K∩B¯R,E:=X∩∂BR.X:=K\cap\overline{B}_{R},\qquad E:=X\cap\partial B_{R}.

The space XX is compact, and C∩E=∅C\cap E=\varnothing. Moreover, CC is a connected component of XX: it is connected and contained in XX, and any connected subset of XX strictly containing CC would also be a connected subset of KK, contradicting the maximality of CC.

We use the standard fact [Eng89, Theorem 6.1.23] that a component of a compact Hausdorff space is the intersection of all subsets containing it that are both open and closed in that space. Thus, for each y∈Ey\in E, there is a set Vy⊂XV_{y}\subset X, open and closed in XX, such that C⊂VyC\subset V_{y} and y∉Vyy\notin V_{y}. The sets X∖VyX\setminus V_{y} form an open cover of EE relative to XX. Since EE is compact, we can choose finitely many y1,…,yN∈Ey_{1},\ldots,y_{N}\in E such that

E⊂⋃i=1N(X∖Vyi),W:=⋂i=1NVyi.E\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}(X\setminus V_{y_{i}}),\qquad W:=\bigcap_{i=1}^{N}V_{y_{i}}.

Then WW is open and closed in XX and contains CC. The covering property gives W∩E=∅W\cap E=\varnothing, so W⊂BRW\subset B_{R}. If E=∅E=\varnothing, take W=XW=X, which has the same properties.

Since WW is closed in the compact space XX, it is compact and hence closed in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, so it is also relatively closed in KK. Since WW is open in XX, write W=O∩XW=O\cap X for some open set O⊂ℝ2O\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}. As W⊂BRW\subset B_{R}, we have

W=K∩(O∩BR),W=K\cap(O\cap B_{R}),

so WW is relatively open in KK. Finally, WW is nonempty because it contains CC. Thus WW is a nonempty compact subset of KK that is both relatively open and relatively closed in KK, contrary to the hypothesis. ∎

Theorem 3.4 (Classification of generalized global minimizers).

Let (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}) be a reduced generalized global minimizer in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Then either ∇u=0\nabla u=0 a.e. on ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K, so that the minimizer is elementary, or (u,K)(u,K) is the canonical crack tip (2.2), up to translation, rotation, sign, and an additive constant.

Proof.

Let (u,K,{pk​l})(u,K,\{p_{kl}\}) be a generalized global minimizer in the sense of [DLF, Definition 2.2.4]. If ℝ2∖K\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus K is disconnected, [DLF, Theorem 4.4.1] gives a pure-jump or triple-junction model. If KK is compact, including K=∅K=\varnothing, [DLF, Theorem 1.4.6, first paragraph] already applies, since all components are contained in a common compact set. Its only model with compact KK is the constant minimizer.

It remains to consider noncompact KK with connected complement. Proposition 3.1 excludes every nonempty compact relatively open-and-closed subset of KK, since any such subset would be proper. Lemma 3.3 therefore makes every component of KK unbounded. By [DLF, Corollary 4.4.3] there is at most one such component, so KK is connected. The classification of generalized global minimizers with connected KK [DLF, Theorem 1.4.6] gives the conclusion. ∎
